vtrmc-1987-01.title: Sum a geometric series
vtrmc-1987-01.body:
$P_1=(\tfrac12,-\tfrac12)$, so $|P_0P_1|=\sqrt{\tfrac14+\tfrac14}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

For $n\ge1$, the horizontal distance from $P_n$ to $P_{n+1}$ is $2^{-n}-2^{-n-1}=2^{-n-1}$. The $y$-coordinates $(-2)^{-n}$ and $(-2)^{-n-1}$ have opposite signs, so the vertical distance is $2^{-n}+2^{-n-1}=3\cdot2^{-n-1}$. Hence
$$|P_nP_{n+1}|=2^{-n-1}\sqrt{1+9}=2^{-n-1}\sqrt{10}.$$
Since $P_n\to(0,0)$, the length of the path is
$$\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\sqrt{10}\sum_{n=1}^\infty2^{-n-1}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}=\frac{\sqrt2+\sqrt{10}}{2}\approx2.288 .$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt2+\sqrt{10}}{2}$.**

vtrmc-1987-01.title: Scaling
vtrmc-1987-01.body:
For $n\ge1$, if $P_n=(x_n,y_n)$ then $P_{n+1}=(\tfrac12x_n,-\tfrac12y_n)$: a reflection in the $x$-axis followed by scaling by $\tfrac12$. So the segment $P_{n+1}P_{n+2}$ is a congruent-up-to-scale copy of $P_nP_{n+1}$ with half the length.

The first such segment is $P_1P_2$ from $(\tfrac12,-\tfrac12)$ to $(\tfrac14,\tfrac14)$, of length $\sqrt{\tfrac1{16}+\tfrac9{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{10}}4$. The total from $P_1$ on is $\frac{\sqrt{10}}4(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\dots)=\frac{\sqrt{10}}2$, and adding $|P_0P_1|=\frac{\sqrt2}2$ gives $\frac{\sqrt2+\sqrt{10}}2$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{\sqrt2+\sqrt{10}}{2}$.**

vtrmc-1987-02.title: Right triangle with integer altitude
vtrmc-1987-02.body:
Let the altitude from the vertex opposite $c$ have length $d$ and divide $c$ into pieces $x$ (next to $a$) and $y$ (next to $b$). Each small triangle has a right angle at the foot of the altitude, so if it is similar to the original triangle, the original is also right-angled, and its right angle must be at the vertex opposite $c$ (the longest side). Then
$$a^2=x^2+d^2,\qquad b^2=y^2+d^2,\qquad a^2+b^2=(x+y)^2 ,$$
and these give $2d^2=2xy$, i.e. $d^2=xy$. Conversely, in a right triangle the altitude to the hypotenuse always produces two triangles similar to the original.

So we need positive integers $x,y,d$ with $d^2=xy$ and $x(x+y)$, $y(x+y)$ perfect squares (these are $a^2$ and $b^2$). Choosing $x,y,x+y$ all perfect squares works: $x=9$, $y=16$, $x+y=25$. Then $d=12$, $a=\sqrt{9\cdot25}=15$, $b=\sqrt{16\cdot25}=20$, $c=25$.

Check: the pieces are the triangles with sides $9,12,15$ and $12,16,20$, both similar to $15,20,25$ (all are multiples of $3,4,5$), with integer sides, and $15<20<25$.

**Answer (one example): $a=15$, $b=20$, $c=25$.**

vtrmc-1987-02.title: Scale a Pythagorean triple
vtrmc-1987-02.body:
As explained, the triangle must be right-angled at the vertex opposite $c$. Start from a Pythagorean triple $(p,q,r)$, $p<q<r$. The altitude to the hypotenuse splits it into triangles with scale factors $\frac pr$ and $\frac qr$ relative to the original, i.e. with sides $\frac{p}{r}(p,q,r)$ and $\frac{q}{r}(p,q,r)$. These are integers if we first multiply the triple by $r$: the triangle $(pr,qr,r^2)$ splits into $(p^2,pq,pr)$ and $(pq,q^2,qr)$.

With $(3,4,5)$: $(a,b,c)=(15,20,25)$, pieces $(9,12,15)$ and $(12,16,20)$. (With $(5,12,13)$ one gets $(65,156,169)$, etc.)

**Answer (one example): $15,20,25$.**

vtrmc-1987-03.title: Pigeonhole on parities
vtrmc-1987-03.body: Let $n=2k+1$. Among $1,\dots,n$ there are $k+1$ odd numbers and $k$ even numbers. The odd values $a_i$ (there are $k+1$ of them) occupy $k+1$ positions $i$, but only $k$ positions are even. Hence some odd value $a_r$ is at an odd position $r$. Then $a_r-r$ is (odd)$-$(odd) $=$ even, so the whole product is even. ∎

vtrmc-1987-03.title: Sum of the factors
vtrmc-1987-03.body:
The sum of the factors is
$$\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i-i)=\sum_{i=1}^na_i-\sum_{i=1}^ni=0,$$
because $(a_i)$ is a rearrangement of $(1,\dots,n)$. If all $n$ factors were odd, their sum would be a sum of an odd number of odd integers, hence odd — but it is $0$, which is even. So at least one factor is even, and the product is even. ∎

vtrmc-1987-04.title: Look near $0$
vtrmc-1987-04.body:
**(a)** At $x=0$: $|a_0|=|p(0)|\le|0|=0$, so $a_0=0$.

**(b)** By (a), $p(x)=x(a_1+a_2x+\dots+a_nx^{n-1})$, so for $x\ne0$
$$\frac{p(x)}{x}=a_1+a_2x+\dots+a_nx^{n-1}\xrightarrow[x\to0]{}a_1 .$$
The hypothesis gives $\left|\frac{p(x)}x\right|\le1$ for $0<|x|\le1$, so the limit satisfies $|a_1|\le1$. ∎

vtrmc-1987-04.title: Derivative at $0$
vtrmc-1987-04.body:
**(a)** As above, $a_0=p(0)=0$.

**(b)** $a_1=p'(0)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{p(h)-p(0)}{h}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{p(h)}h$. Since $|p(h)|\le|h|$, each difference quotient lies in $[-1,1]$, and so does its limit: $|a_1|\le1$. (Equality is possible, e.g. $p(x)=x$.) ∎

vtrmc-1987-05.title: Monotone and bounded
vtrmc-1987-05.body:
We take $n_1\ge0$ (binary representations are of non-negative integers). For $k\ge2$,
$$n_{k+1}=n_k+z(n_k),$$
since $n_{k+1}-n_k=z(n_k)$.

**(a)** Take $n_1=2^{31}$, whose binary representation is $1$ followed by $31$ zeros. Then $n_2=z(n_1)=31=11111_2$, and $z(31)=0$, so $n_3=n_2+0=31$, and inductively $n_k=31$ for all $k\ge2$:
$$n_2=n_3=\dots=n_{10}=31,$$
and $\lim n_k=31$.

**(b)** For $k\ge2$ the sequence is non-decreasing since $z\ge0$. If some $n_k=0$ ($k\ge2$), then $n_{k+1}=0+z(0)=1$ and $z(1)=0$, so the sequence is constant $1$ afterwards. Otherwise let $k\ge2$ and $2^m\le n_k<2^{m+1}$, so $n_k$ has $m+1$ binary digits, $\ell=z(n_k)$ of which are $0$. Each zero digit in position $i$ makes $n_k$ smaller than $2^{m+1}-1=11\dots1_2$ by $2^i\ge1$, so
$$n_k\le 2^{m+1}-1-\ell,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad n_{k+1}=n_k+\ell\le2^{m+1}-1 .$$
So $n_{k+1}$ again lies in $[2^m,2^{m+1})$, and by induction all later terms do. A non-decreasing sequence of integers bounded above is eventually constant, so $\{n_k\}$ converges. ∎

vtrmc-1987-06.title: $x=-1$ is always a root
vtrmc-1987-06.body:
$(a_n)$ is the Fibonacci sequence $1,1,2,3,5,\dots$, so $a_n>0$. Since
$$p_n(-1)=a_{n+2}-a_{n+1}-a_n=0,$$
$x=-1$ is a root of every $p_n$. The product of the roots is $-\frac{a_n}{a_{n+2}}<0$, so the other root is $\frac{a_n}{a_{n+2}}>0>-1$. Hence
$$r_n=-1,\qquad s_n=\frac{a_n}{a_{n+2}} .$$
Let $f=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}$. This limit exists and equals $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ (Binet: $a_n=\frac{\varphi^{n+1}-\psi^{n+1}}{\sqrt5}$ with $\psi=\frac{1-\sqrt5}2$, $|\psi|<1$); it satisfies $f^2=f+1$, $f>0$. Therefore
$$\lim s_n=\lim\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}\cdot\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n+2}}=\frac1{\varphi^2}=\frac1{\varphi+1}=\frac{2}{3+\sqrt5}=\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}.$$

**Answer: $\lim r_n=-1$, $\lim s_n=\frac{3-\sqrt5}2\approx0.382$.**

vtrmc-1987-06.title: Limit of the polynomials
vtrmc-1987-06.body:
Divide $p_n$ by $a_n>0$: the roots of $p_n$ are the roots of
$$\frac{a_{n+2}}{a_n}x^2+\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}x-1 ,$$
whose coefficients tend to $\varphi^2$, $\varphi$, $-1$ (with $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$). The roots depend continuously on the coefficients (the leading coefficient stays away from $0$ and the discriminant stays positive), so they tend to the roots of $\varphi^2x^2+\varphi x-1=0$:
$$x=\frac{-\varphi\pm\sqrt{\varphi^2+4\varphi^2}}{2\varphi^2}=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt5}{2\varphi}=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt5}{1+\sqrt5}.$$
The minus sign gives $-1$, the plus sign $\frac{\sqrt5-1}{\sqrt5+1}=\frac{(\sqrt5-1)^2}{4}=\frac{3-\sqrt5}2$.

**Answer: $-1$ and $\frac{3-\sqrt5}2$.**

vtrmc-1987-07.title: Multiply by a diagonal matrix
vtrmc-1987-07.body:
Let $D$ be the diagonal matrix with $d_{nn}=t$ and $d_{ii}=1$ for $i<n$. Multiplying a matrix on the left by $D$ multiplies its last row by $t$ and leaves the other rows unchanged, so
$$A(t)=DA,\qquad B(t)=DB .$$
For $t>0$, $D$ is invertible ($\det D=t\ne0$), hence $A(t)=DA$ is invertible with $A(t)^{-1}=A^{-1}D^{-1}$. Therefore
$$A(t)^{-1}B(t)=A^{-1}D^{-1}DB=A^{-1}B.$$
∎

vtrmc-1987-07.title: Via linear systems
vtrmc-1987-07.body: $X=A^{-1}B$ is the unique matrix with $AX=B$ (column by column: $AX_j=B_j$ for the columns). Multiplying the last equation of each system $AX_j=B_j$ by $t\ne0$ does not change its solution set, and produces exactly the systems $A(t)X_j=B(t)_j$. Also $\det A(t)=t\det A\ne0$, so $A(t)$ is invertible and $A(t)^{-1}B(t)$ is the unique solution of $A(t)X=B(t)$, which is therefore $X=A^{-1}B$. ∎

vtrmc-1987-08.title: Linear system with complex eigenvalues
vtrmc-1987-08.body:
**(a)** The witch's velocity points from her to the cat and has length equal to their distance, so it is the vector cat $-$ witch: $x'=u-x$, $y'=v-y$. The apparent (mirror-image) position of the witch is $(-x,y)$, so the cat's velocity is $(-x,y)-(u,v)$:
$$x'=u-x,\quad y'=v-y,\quad u'=-x-u,\quad v'=y-v .$$

**(b)** The pair $(u,x)$ satisfies $Y'=AY$ with
$$Y=\begin{pmatrix}u\\x\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$
The eigenvalues of $A$ are $-1\pm i$, so the solutions are $e^{-t}$ times combinations of $\cos t$ and $\sin t$. Write $u=e^{-t}(\alpha\cos t+\beta\sin t)$; then $x=-u'-u$, and
$$u'=e^{-t}\big((\beta-\alpha)\cos t-(\alpha+\beta)\sin t\big),\qquad x=-u-u'=e^{-t}(-\beta\cos t+\alpha\sin t).$$
The initial values $u(0)=10$, $x(0)=10$ give $\alpha=10$, $\beta=-10$:
$$u(t)=10e^{-t}(\cos t-\sin t),\qquad x(t)=10e^{-t}(\cos t+\sin t).$$
(Check: $u'=-20e^{-t}\cos t=-x-u$ and $x'=-20e^{-t}\sin t=u-x$.)

The cat strikes the mirror when $u(t)=0$ for the first time, i.e. $\cos t=\sin t$:
$$t=\frac\pi4 .$$

**Answer: $u=10e^{-t}(\cos t-\sin t)$, $x=10e^{-t}(\cos t+\sin t)$, and the cat hits the mirror at $t=\pi/4$.**

vtrmc-1987-08.title: Complex variable
vtrmc-1987-08.body:
Put $w=x+iu$. Since
$$-(1+i)w=-(1+i)(x+iu)=-x-iu-ix+u=(u-x)+i(-x-u)=x'+iu',$$
we have $w'=-(1+i)w$, so
$$w(t)=w(0)e^{-(1+i)t}=(10+10i)e^{-t}(\cos t-i\sin t)=10e^{-t}\big[(\cos t+\sin t)+i(\cos t-\sin t)\big].$$
Reading off real and imaginary parts: $x=10e^{-t}(\cos t+\sin t)$, $u=10e^{-t}(\cos t-\sin t)$. Also $\arg w(0)=\frac\pi4$ and $\arg w(t)=\frac\pi4-t$, so $u=\operatorname{Im}w$ first vanishes when $t=\frac\pi4$.

**Answer: the cat strikes the mirror at $t=\pi/4$.**
